name: Marco Ziegler

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for sitting down with me, Marco. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or parties. Everything you tell me is confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Can you walk me through a normal day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at Kessel's, a busy independent garage on the high street with five bays. Last spring the owner bought an AI diagnostic system that listens to the engine and reads all the sensor data, and somehow I became the person who runs it, because I'm the only one who wasn't scared of it. So half my day I'm plugging cars in and explaining to the older lads what it says, and the other half I'm doing services and getting told my torque work is sloppy. Fair enough, I'm still learning the spanner side.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with my partner Ines, who's a physiotherapist. At weekends I do mobile servicing out of my own van, oil and filters on people's driveways, which pays for our holidays. Between that and my savings we're comfortable. I use AI for everything, honestly, from planning my weekend jobs to checking parts prices.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Here's the card: “Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm a bit disappointed but not surprised. The diagnostic box is good, but it's not magic, and I'd say that at work. Online I'd probably post a tip about how to get the most out of the tools anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it'd be fine for me. I'd lose a bit of the edge I have from being the AI guy at Kessel's, but mechanics are always in demand. My weekend work would carry on as it is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd focus on getting better at the hands-on stuff, because that's where I'm weak, and ask Stefan, the head mechanic, to check my work more. I'd grow the weekend servicing a little, maybe two extra jobs a month. And I'd keep investing in a global index fund like I do now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It's comfortable. A bit boring, maybe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the routine tasks AI takes over touch anything in your day?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mainly the paperwork. The system already writes the job notes for me, and booking my weekend customers is automated. That just gives me more time under the cars.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you worry about already, AI aside?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Being average forever, I suppose. I'm good with the computers and below par with the spanners, and garages pay for spanners. That's on me to fix.

I'd post **tips** online about getting the most from the tools anyway.
think: I'd lose some of my **edge** as the garage's AI guy, but mechanics stay in demand.
My **weekend servicing** would carry on as it is.
do: Ask the head mechanic to **check his work** and improve his hands-on skill.
Add **two extra** weekend servicing jobs a month.
Keep investing in a **global index fund**.
feel: **Calm** and comfortable, maybe a little bored.

fieldNote: He's the garage's **AI guy** despite being the junior.

Weekend **mobile servicing** gives him a second income already.

steps.text: Ask the head mechanic to check his torque work on every service
Take on two more weekend driveway servicing jobs a month
Keep paying into the global index fund

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Here's the card: “Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a good time for people who learn the tools, and I'd tell others to start now. At work I'd offer to show the older lads how to use the system properly. Online I'd post short how-to videos.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'd do well. Diagnosis, quoting and ordering all go. The thinking side of a garage goes to AI, and I'm the one at our garage who already runs it. Robots come slowly for hands-on work, so my job is safe and probably gets more important.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the owner for a pay rise and a new title, something like diagnostic lead, because I'm already doing it. I'd add AI quoting and booking to my weekend business so I can take more jobs. And I'd do a hybrid and EV course so the hands-on side keeps up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and honestly excited. It feels like a door opening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at Kessel's would struggle?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Stefan, the head mechanic, maybe. He's brilliant with his hands but hates screens. If the owner starts judging everyone by what the system says, Stefan looks slower than he is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ever leave Kessel's in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe, for a bigger garage chain that wants someone to run AI diagnostics across several sites. That would pay more. But I'd want to be properly good at the spanner side first.

I'd post **how-to videos** and offer to train older colleagues.

Take a **hybrid and EV** course to strengthen hands-on skills.

steps.text: Run the AI diagnostic system and train older colleagues on it

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Here's the card: “Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's too fast and companies and government need to cushion it for people. I'd still tell people to learn the tools, because two years is better spent learning than worrying. I'd probably post a lot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think my edge disappears quickly. If AI can do any thinking work by 2028, then being the guy who runs the diagnostic system isn't special. It's just a button. And by 2031 the robots do the spanner work I'm already weak at, when I'm thirty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the next two years to earn as much as possible, doing more weekend jobs. I'd move some savings out of the index fund into a small rental property with Ines, because people will still need homes. And I'd look at work maintaining or supervising robots in garages, since someone will have to set them up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I like change, but this is change with no room to breathe. Ines's job feels safer than mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why is Ines's job safer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Physio is hands on people, not cars. People will want a person touching their bad knee for longer than they'll want a person fixing their gearbox. That's my guess, anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you like change. Is that still true here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly. I'd be the first to try the robot bays, I'd probably even enjoy it. But liking the tools doesn't mean the tools need me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Here's the card: “Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a decent window and people should start learning now. I'd keep posting tips. At work I'd be pushing the owner to plan ahead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, five years is good for me. I'd have until about 2034 before robots do the hands-on work. That's time to get good with the spanners, move up to diagnostic lead, and then learn robot maintenance before anyone else around here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get the EV qualification in the first year and push for diagnostic lead. Around 2030 I'd do a robotics maintenance course, part-time. I'd keep the weekend van going and maybe hire a friend for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. I'd feel like I'm ahead, but I know everyone else will catch up eventually.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you hire someone for the van business?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe my mate Luka, who's also a mechanic and wants more weekend money. If I'm busy with courses, he could do half the jobs. It's a small step towards running something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to the owner of Kessel's about planning ahead?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my boss to start thinking about robot bays by 2032, or he'll be beaten by the chains. He'd say I'm getting ahead of myself. He'd probably be right, but someone has to say it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Here's the card: “Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is great, there's no excuse not to be ready. I'd tell younger mechanics to learn both the tools and the hands-on side. Online I'd post about how the trade will change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be very relaxed. Robots around 2039, I'd be forty. I'd build my skills, maybe open a small garage of my own, and bring in robots myself when they're ready.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at Kessel's for a few years, get good, then open a small garage around 2031 with my savings. I'd automate the booking and diagnosis from day one. When the robots come, I'd rather buy them for my own garage than be replaced by them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Excited, really. It's a long runway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much would opening a garage cost you, roughly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe sixty or seventy thousand for a small unit and kit, I'd guess. I'd need a loan on top of savings. Ten years of steady work makes that realistic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about it that still bothers you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If I'm the one buying robots, I'm the one deciding who to let go. That's not nice to think about. But I'd rather be making the choice than having it made for me.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because being good at AI stops being special overnight. What would help is cheap loans for small garages to buy the new kit, so it's not just the chains. And proper courses for robot maintenance, early.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Whether people trust a car fixed by a robot. Customers already ask me if the diagnostic box is right, so I think trust will take longer than the technology.

portrait: Marco is a **junior mechanic** at a five-bay high-street garage who runs its AI diagnostic system.
He's weak on the **spanner side** and knows it, but uses AI for everything.
He earns extra from **weekend mobile servicing** and lives with a physiotherapist partner.
He stays **calm** in most pictures and turns anxious only at two years.
He wants to **own a garage** and buy robots rather than be replaced.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because his AI skills stop being special overnight.
whatWouldHelp: **Cheap loans** for small garages to buy new kit.
